analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal oversight of large systemically important nonbank financial firms under Dodd-Frank.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, died in the House Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote, leaving Dodd-Frank's supervision of large nonbank financial firms in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stripped the Federal Reserve of its authority to supervise large nonbank financial companies — insurers, finance companies, and similar firms that are not banks but whose failure could shake the whole financial system. It would also have wiped out the Financial Stability Oversight Council's power to designate which firms get that extra scrutiny, eliminated their reporting and 'living will' requirements, and repealed the law setting risk-management standards for payment, clearing, and settlement systems. In short, it unwound a core piece of the post-2008 rules that put the biggest financial firms under closer watch.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders and executives of the largest nonbank financial companies — big insurers, finance companies, and asset managers — would gain the most: they would be freed from Federal Reserve supervision, heightened capital and leverage standards, mandatory resolution plans, periodic exposure reports, and the ban on management interlocks with other financial companies [S2] [S3]. Clearinghouses and settlement systems would also be freed from federal risk-management oversight [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large nonbank financial firms and clearinghouses

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates all Federal Reserve supervision of domestic and foreign nonbank financial companies, including heightened standards and minimum leverage capital requirements [S2] [S3].

Removes the Financial Stability Oversight Council's authority to identify systemically important firms and market utilities, and repeals its power to require resolution plans ('living wills') and credit-exposure reporting from nonbank companies [S2] [S3].
Repeals the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act of 2010, which set risk-management standards for the utilities that process payments and trades [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary households and taxpayers would bear the added risk. The 2008 crisis showed that the failure of a nonbank firm like AIG could threaten the entire financial system and force government rescues. Removing the extra capital, reporting, and resolution-planning rules for these firms would make such failures — and the taxpayer-backed bailouts that follow them — more likely, while doing nothing to lower the cost of everyday banking or credit.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the underlying Dodd-Frank provisions argued that without them, large nonbank firms could take the same risks banks took before 2008 with no extra capital cushion or plan for winding themselves down, leaving taxpayers exposed again [S2].

A good-faith objection the bill embodied: designation as 'systemically important' can itself signal a government backstop, potentially giving designated firms a funding advantage and encouraging bigness — so repealing designation could reduce that implicit subsidy, at the cost of removing real supervision [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear benefit to a narrow set of very large financial firms — lower supervisory costs and fewer constraints — while shifting the downside risk of a systemic failure back onto taxpayers and the broader economy. The history of the 2008 crisis, which the Dodd-Frank provisions were written to address, makes that trade a poor one for ordinary people; the bill's own argument about implicit bailout subsidies addresses a real concern but does not justify removing capital and resolution-planning rules entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Garrett (R-NJ) introduced the bill on August 2, 2012 [S1] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors from either party [S4].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died in committee without a vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Dodd-Frank supervision of large nonbank financial firms — extra capital standards, resolution plans, and Council designation authority — remained in place for the time being. The beneficiaries of the bill dying were ordinary households and taxpayers, who kept safeguards against a repeat of the kind of nonbank failure seen with AIG in 2008; the large nonbank financial firms the bill was written for did not get the relief it promised.

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Federal Reserve supervision of nonbank financial companies and the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Spencer Bachus (R) during the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for consideration; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican introduced the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and no recorded vote ever tested where the parties stood [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (systemically important insurers, finance companies, and asset managers)
industries.note: The bill would free these firms from Federal Reserve supervision, heightened capital and leverage standards, resolution-plan and exposure-reporting requirements, and the management interlock ban — the core Dodd-Frank rules written after AIG's 2008 collapse showed nonbank failures can threaten the whole system. Their cost savings come at the price of greater bailout risk for taxpayers.

Repealing the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act removes federal risk-management standards for the infrastructure that processes payments and trades. The savings accrue to the utilities; the added fragility in the plumbing of the financial system falls on everyone who uses it.
